title: Behaviour-Driven, Explainable Reconnaissance Detection and the Inflation of Its Metrics: A Cross-Dataset Study on UNSW-NB15 and IoT-23
content: Machine-learning network intrusion detection systems routinely report near-perfect scores. This paper is primarily methodological: using a lightweight, interpretable detector for the Reconnaissance phase as a controlled test bed, built on eight manually selected behavioural features with per-alert SHAP explanations, we measure how such scores become inflated and which diagnostics expose it. Every quantitative claim is averaged over repeated random seeds with paired significance tests. We examine three mechanisms. First, duplicate contamination: 38.6% of UNSW-NB15 records are exact duplicates once projected onto the eight features, and 46% of Reconnaissance records in a held-out test fold have an identical twin in the training fold; evaluating the same model at the same threshold on twin-free records alone drops the Reconnaissance F1 from 0.759±0.034 to 0.622±0.041 (p&lt;0.001), with recall falling ten points. Second, base-rate inflation: transferred to IoT-23, whose evaluation set is 90.75% Reconnaissance, the detector reaches an apparent precision of 0.924±0.026; subsampling that set to the in-domain prevalence of 0.62%, with the model and threshold unchanged, collapses precision to 0.009±0.004. Third, test-set leakage in threshold selection, which an earlier version of this work reported as material: over thirty seeds it is +0.0001±0.0159 (p=0.35), and we report that non-replication in full. An ablation retrained on the features shared by both datasets still fails to transfer, so the cross-dataset failure reflects distribution shift rather than our feature substitution. Two limitations bound these conclusions: three of the eight features cannot be derived from Zeek logs and are substituted by constants, and roughly 75% of IoT-23 records are discarded for missing fields. We argue that honest NIDS evaluation requires duplicate auditing on the modelling feature space, explicit prevalence reporting, threshold-independent metrics, held-out threshold selection and repeated-run uncertainty estimates.
